Empirical Research Plan  
“Rain, Banks and the Rural Labour Market:  India 1956-1987”

────────────────────────────────────────

1. Identification Strategy  
Method:  Panel Difference-in-Differences with an instrumental-variables extension (“triple-difference 2SLS”).

•  Step 1 (first stage) Crop productivity (log yield of the five major crops, Y idt) is instrumented with growing-season rainfall anomalies R idt.  
•  Step 2 (reduced form) District-year agricultural wages w idt are regressed on the predicted yield shocks Ŷ idt.  
•  Step 3 (heterogeneity / triple-diff) Ŷ idt is interacted with time-invariant proxies for consumption-smoothing ability (financial development, outward migration possibilities, poverty, landlessness).  

Why appropriate?  
– Rainfall variation within a small geographical unit and within a short time-window is plausibly random.  
– 1956-87 gives a long balanced panel, enabling district and year fixed effects to soak up permanent cross-district wage gaps and nationwide macro shocks.  
– IV filters out any direct dis-utility or measurement-error effects of rainfall on wages that do not operate through farm productivity.  
– Interactions deliver differential effects that speak directly to the amplifying role of “underdevelopment” features.

────────────────────────────────────────

2. Treatment and Control

Continuous “treatment”:  District-year productivity shock Ŷ idt (predicted log yield from first-stage).  
Control:  District-years experiencing smaller (or opposite-signed) predicted yield shocks in the same year.  
Timing:  Annual, assigned at the end of each agricultural year (July–June) to avoid overlap of monsoon seasons.  
No discrete cutoff, so no RDD running variable.

Key heterogeneity variables (measured pre-period or averaged 1956-60 to avoid endogeneity):
•  FINi = log(bank branches per 1000 persons) – financial access  
•  MIGi = log(distance to nearest city × inverse bus frequency) – migration friction  
•  POVi = poverty headcount rate (1987-88 NSS)  
•  LANDi = landlessness share or land-Gini (1981 Agricultural Census)

────────────────────────────────────────

3. Key Identifying Assumptions

A1.  Quasi-random rainfall:  Conditional on district and year fixed effects, rainfall anomalies are orthogonal to unobserved determinants of wages.  
Plausibility:  Monsoon timing is meteorologically driven; man-made irrigation below 600 m was limited during the sample period.

A2.  Exclusion (IV):  Rainfall affects wages only through agricultural productivity, not via other channels after conditioning on controls.  
Plausibility:  Remaining channels (e.g. rain-damaged roads) are short-lived; will test by including contemporaneous rainfall itself in the second stage.

A3.  No differential pre-trends between high- and low-financial-development districts.  
Plausibility:  District FEs absorb permanent wage differences; event-study coefficients on leads of rainfall will be plotted as a diagnostic.

A4.  Heterogeneity regressors are predetermined and slow-moving.  
Plausibility:  Banking expansion after 1969 “branch-licensing” was partially policy-driven; we will instrument FINi with 1961 branch density interacted with national branch-expansion waves as a robustness.

A5.  Limited spatial spillovers:  Workers cannot instantly reallocate across ≥50 km to arbitrage wages.  
Plausibility:  Most rural workers faced high migration costs; we will cluster standard errors at the agro-climatic-zone × year level to be conservative.

────────────────────────────────────────

4. Main Threats & Mitigation

T1.  Direct rainfall effects on labour dis-utility or measurement error.  
 •  Mitigation:  Include contemporaneous rainfall and its square in the second stage; restrict instrument to rainfall during pre-harvest months only.

T2.  Endogenous banking growth (high-rainfall districts attract banks).  
 •  Mitigation:  Use pre-period FINi; instrument FINi as noted above; re-estimate dropping post-1969 years when differential branch licensing was strongest.

T3.  Migration spillovers dilute wage effects.  
 •  Mitigation:  (i) Include district-group-by-year FEs at the agro-climatic-zone level; (ii) exploit ICRISAT village survey to show that out-migration rises after bad rainfall only in high-connectivity locations; include migration variables as controls.

────────────────────────────────────────

5. R Code Outline

```r
# 0. Packages ------------------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)      # fast data handling
library(fixest)          # OLS and IV with high-dim FE
library(readr)

# 1. Load data -----------------------------------------------------------
wage   <- fread("district_wage_1956_1987.csv")        # main panel
yield  <- fread("district_crop_yield.csv")            # crop yields
rain   <- fread("district_rainfall.csv")              # growing-season rain
chars  <- fread("district_chars_static.csv")          # FINi, MIGi, POVi, LANDi

# 2. Merge & construct variables ----------------------------------------
panel <- Reduce(function(x,y) merge(x,y, by=c("district","year"), all=TRUE),
                list(wage, yield, rain))[
                 , log_wage := log(male_daily_wage)
               ][ , log_yield := log(sum_yield_majorcrops) ]

# rainfall anomaly: deviation from district mean
panel[, rain_dev := (rain_gs - mean(rain_gs), by=district)]
panel[, rain_z   := scale(rain_dev), by=district]

# attach time-invariant characteristics
panel <- merge(panel, chars, by="district")

# interactions
panel[, `:=`(pred = NA_real_,
             FIN_int  = 0, MIG_int = 0, POV_int = 0, LAND_int = 0)]

# 3. First stage: yield on rainfall -------------------------------------
fs <- feols(log_yield ~ rain_z | district + year, data = panel)
panel[, pred := predict(fs)]  # store fitted values

# 4. Main 2SLS with heterogeneity ---------------------------------------
# Example: financial development heterogeneity
iv_main <- feols(log_wage ~ 1 | district + year | 
                 log_yield ~ rain_z + rain_z:FINi,  # second term gives interaction
                 data = panel, cluster = ~district)

summary(iv_main)

# 5. Robustness: include rain directly ----------------------------------
iv_rb <- feols(log_wage ~ rain_z + I(rain_z^2) | district + year |
               log_yield ~ rain_z, data = panel, cluster = ~district)
summary(iv_rb)

# 6. Event-study pre-trend check ----------------------------------------
panel[, lead2 := shift(rain_z, 2L, type="lead"), by=district]
pretrend <- feols(log_wage ~ l(rain_z, 3:1) + rain_z + f(rain_z,1:3) |
                  district + year, data = panel)
etable(pretrend)
```

────────────────────────────────────────

6. Expected Results

Economic intuition (Bardhan 1984; Basu 1997) predicts:

•  Elasticity of wages to productivity shocks is positive but < 1.  
•  In districts with weak consumption-smoothing (low FINi, high POVi, long MIG distance, high landlessness) the elasticity will be larger because labour supply is less able to smooth inter-temporally or across space.

Illustrative magnitude:  
– High-finance districts:  Δlog wage / Δlog yield ≈ 0.30  
– Low-finance districts:  Δlog wage / Δlog yield ≈ 0.60  
A one-standard-deviation negative rainfall shock (~-20 %) would therefore cut daily wages by ≈ 12 % in low-finance areas versus 6 % in high-finance areas.

────────────────────────────────────────

7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (1 = met, 0 = doubtful)

C1:  Parallel trends (checked with pre-trend plot) .............. 0.8  
C2:  Exogeneity of instrument (rainfall) ........................ 0.9  
C3:  Exclusion restriction (rain ⟹ yield ⟹ wage only) .......... 0.7  
C4:  No spillovers / SUTVA ...................................... 0.6  
C5:  Stable unit composition (wage series consistent) ........... 0.9  

Overall average ≈ 0.78 → Reasonably credible but not bullet-proof.

────────────────────────────────────────
